questions.question: Is copper actually necessary for the body, or is it just a contaminant?
questions.answer: Copper is an essential metal, not only a contaminant. It is required by enzymes including cytochrome c oxidase, lysyl oxidase, and Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle & Barchowsky 2021]]. The concern arises from excess rather than from copper being present at all.

questions.question: What happens if you get too much copper?
questions.answer: Excess copper can produce gastrointestinal and hepatic (liver) toxicity [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle & Barchowsky 2021]]. The page frames this as an effect of excess copper, in contrast to copper's essential role at normal levels.

questions.question: Are there genetic conditions that affect how the body handles copper?
questions.answer: Yes. Inherited copper-metabolism disorders include Menkes disease and Wilson disease [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle & Barchowsky 2021]]. These are disorders of copper metabolism rather than dietary-exposure effects.
